title: The Temple Is Not a Hideout
sum: Jeremiah stands at the gate of the Temple and tells the worshipers that their favorite slogan is a lie. "The LORD's temple, the LORD's temple, the LORD's temple" will not protect them, because they steal, murder, swear falsely and burn smoke to Baal, and then walk into God's house and say "We are rescued." He sends them to Shiloh, where the LORD once had his house and let it be destroyed. If they change their ways and treat the foreigner, the orphan and the widow fairly, they can stay in the land. If not, Jerusalem will go the way of Shiloh.

The rest of the chapter shows how far things have gone. The LORD tells Jeremiah to stop praying for the people (7:16). Whole families bake cakes for the Queen of Heaven (7:18). The LORD says he never gave orders about burnt offerings and sacrifice, only the order to listen (7:22–23). The chapter ends in a funeral song and a vision of the Valley of Ben-hinnom, where children were burned, turned into a Valley of Slaughter (7:29–34).
readings: Read as history

The sermon was given in the first months of Jehoiakim's reign, about 609 BC, when Josiah's death at Megiddo had shaken the hope that the reformed Temple guaranteed safety. Chapter 26 tells what it cost Jeremiah. Within a generation, in 597 and again in 586, the first deportation and then the burning of the Temple proved the warning right.
Read as a sermon for later readers

Many scholars think the prose here was shaped by editors after the fall, in the style of Deuteronomy, so that exiles could see why the Temple fell: not because God was weak, but because the covenant was broken. The same words then served a new purpose, to teach that worship without justice fails.

views.H: The sermon belongs to the dangerous years after Josiah's death (609 BC), when the Temple was called unshakable. Shiloh, the hope of Hezekiah's deliverance in 701, and the fall of the north in 722 are the three events the audience knew. The chapter is the book's central argument that the Temple cannot protect a nation that breaks the covenant, which is what happened in 586.
views.C: Chapter 7 is mostly prose in the style of the Deuteronomistic editors. Scholars divide on whether it is Jeremiah's own sermon (Bright, Holladay) or a later composition built on a core (Thiel, Nicholson). The Greek is shorter by many small phrases and lacks 7:1, the start of 7:2 and all of 7:27, so the long Hebrew text probably grew. The statement about burnt offerings (7:22) is also read as evidence on when the sacrifice laws of Leviticus took their present form.
views.J: Jewish tradition reads the chapter as one of the clearest statements that obedience matters more than offerings. Rashi reads 7:22 as saying the exodus-day condition was obedience (Exodus 19:5). Radak argues that the Ten Commandments never mention sacrifice. In the Ashkenazi custom, 7:21–8:3 with 9:22–23 (Hebrew numbering; English 9:23–24) is the reading from the prophets (haftarah) for the Torah portion Tzav, which deals with sacrifices. The Sephardi custom reads 7:21–28 with 9:22–23.
views.X: Jesus used 7:11 when he drove the traders from the Temple (Matthew 21:13; Mark 11:17; Luke 19:46) and spoke of the Temple's fall (Mark 13:2). Christians have read 7:22–23 as the prophets' witness that God wants a heart and not a ritual, and Christians still ask how the Queen of Heaven in 7:18 bears on the Marian title (see the card below).

deep.h: Which witnesses I read for chapters 7–12
deep.b: The Plain English Translation follows the Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex). I read the Greek in Swete's printed text of Codex Vaticanus; where this page says "the Greek," it means that text, and a critical edition such as Ziegler's may differ in details. I read the Dead Sea scrolls in the Abegg–Bowley–Cook transcription: 4QJer-a (4Q70) has parts of every chapter here, 4QJer-b (4Q71) has parts of 9:23–10:21 (it ends at 10:21), 4QJer-c (4Q72) has small pieces of 8:1–3, 8:21–22, 9:1–6 and 10:12–13. Their readings are given only where the letters are not restored. The transcription also prints lone-letter signs in 4QJer-a at 7:30, 7:31, 7:33 and 8:1–3; these are not words, and no reading is taken from them. I read Rashi and Radak on Jeremiah in the English on Sefaria for the verses where they are cited. Where a reading rests on someone else's report, the note names the source.

deep.h: What the Greek leaves out in chapter 7
deep.b: Besides the whole verses shown in the variants (7:1, most of 7:2, 7:27), the Greek lacks many small phrases that the Hebrew has. For example it lacks "of Armies" in 7:3 (it has "the Lord, the God of Israel"), has only "the Lord" at 7:21, and shortens 7:2 to "Hear the word of the Lord, all Judah." These do not change the meaning and are not listed one by one. They are part of the pattern that makes the Greek about one-seventh shorter than the Hebrew.

The best argument against the slogan is a place the audience could visit. Shiloh had been Israel's sanctuary in the days of Eli and Samuel (1 Samuel 1–4; Psalm 78:60). It was gone. Archaeologists found a burned city there from about 1050 BC. Jeremiah's logic is not that the Temple is unholy, but that holiness does not work like a charm. When the same city's leaders heard it in chapter 26, some wanted him killed and others recalled that Micah had said the same of Zion in Hezekiah's day (26:16–19).

echoes: Jeremiah 26:1–19; 1 Samuel 4; Psalm 78:60–64; Isaiah 56:7; Matthew 21:13; Mark 11:17; Mark 13:2; 2 Kings 23:10; Deuteronomy 28:26

settings.to: The people of Judah entering the Temple gates to worship
settings.when: Dated by chapter 26 to the beginning of Jehoiakim's reign, about 609 BC; 7:2 sets it in the gate of the LORD's house, and 26:2 says people came from all the cities of Judah to worship, but neither verse names a festival
settings.why: To break the false confidence of the slogan "the LORD's temple" and to offer a last condition: change your ways and the LORD will let you stay. The warning is aimed at people who treat the building as protection while breaking the covenant outside it. Knowing the audience shows that the sermon is not against worship but against worship used as an alibi.
settings.readers: For exiles reading it after 586, the sermon explained why the Temple fell and answered the question whether the LORD had been defeated.
views: Many scholars read 7:1–15 and 26:1–6 as one speech told twice, the sermon here and the story of what followed in 26.
Others think this is a longer or earlier sermon (perhaps under Josiah) and that chapter 26 reports only part of it.

settings.what: The ban on prayer and the Queen of Heaven
settings.when: Not dated. The verbs are singular, so the words are addressed to Jeremiah; whether he heard them at the same time as the sermon is not said
settings.why: To tell the prophet that intercession has no more chance, and to show him why: whole households are worshiping another god. Knowing it was addressed to Jeremiah alone shows that this is not advice to the people to stop praying, but a sign to the prophet of the verdict.

settings.to: The worshipers of Judah, bringing offerings
settings.when: Part of the Temple address, or an added word to it
settings.why: To say that the covenant began with the command to listen, and that offerings given with disobedience please no one. It answers the people who thought that more sacrifices could make up for broken laws.
views: Whether 7:22 denies that God commanded sacrifice at all, or only puts it second to obedience, is discussed in the note.

settings.to: Daughter Zion, the city personified (the verbs are feminine), and the people of Judah
settings.when: As the sermon turns to judgment, in the years before 597 and 586
settings.why: To tell the city to mourn in advance, and to name the Valley of Ben-hinnom as the place where the nation's worst sin will be judged. It makes the valley a warning for Jerusalem.

traditions.q: Is it idolatry to call Mary 'Queen of Heaven'?
views: No. Mary is a creature, honored and not worshiped. The Catechism says she was taken up into heavenly glory and exalted by the Lord as Queen over all things (966, citing Lumen Gentium 59), and that devotion to her differs in kind from the adoration given to God (971). Pius XII set up the feast of her Queenship in 1954 (Ad Caeli Reginam). Teachers such as Scott Hahn root the title in the Davidic queen mother (1 Kings 2:19), not in the goddess of Jeremiah.

Orthodox hymns for the feast of the Dormition call Mary 'Queen' (the Lamentations for the Theotokos say heaven receives 'her Queen' and call her 'Sovereign Queen and Mother of God'), and honor her as Theotokos, 'God-bearer.'

The Lutheran confessions call Mary the blessed Virgin, 'most worthy of the most ample honors,' and hold her up as an example of faith (Apology XXI), but they reject praying to saints, because Scripture 'sets before us the one Christ as the Mediator' (Augsburg Confession XXI). They grant that the blessed Virgin and the saints may pray for the church in general, and they do not teach the title 'Queen of Heaven.'

Religious worship is to be given to God 'and to him alone; not to angels, saints, or any other creature,' and not 'in the mediation of any other but of Christ alone' (Westminster Confession 21.2). The Heidelberg Catechism, Q. 94, lists 'invocation of saints, or any other creatures' among the sins forbidden by the first commandment.

Article XXII of the Thirty-Nine Articles (titled 'Of Purgatory') calls 'the Romish Doctrine concerning Purgatory, Pardons, Worshipping, and Adoration, as well of Images as of Reliques, and also invocation of Saints' a 'fond thing vainly invented.' It does not mention Mary or the title. The Book of Common Prayer also keeps 'The Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin Mary,' as the Church of England's website lists it.
The Second London Baptist Confession (1689) gives worship and prayer to God alone, and not to angels, saints or any other creature (22.2).

traditions.q: 2 Maccabees 15:14 shows Jeremiah praying for the people after his death. Do the saints in heaven pray for the living?
views: Yes, and Christians may ask the saints to pray for them. The Catechism says the saints in heaven keep interceding with the Father for us (956), and the Council of Trent calls it good and useful to ask for their help (Session 25). 2 Maccabees is in the Catholic canon (Trent, Session 4), and it is one of the texts cited.
Yes. The Church's services ask for the prayers of the saints. The troparion of the Dormition tells the Theotokos that by her prayers she delivers our souls from death.

The Lutheran confessions grant that the saints in heaven may pray for the church in general, but they reject calling on them, because Scripture does not command it and Christ is the one mediator (Augsburg Confession XXI; Apology XXI). They take the prophetic and apostolic writings of the Old and New Testaments as the only rule, so 2 Maccabees does not settle the question for them.

The Reformed confessions rule out asking the saints: prayer is made to God alone through Christ (Westminster Confession 21.2; Heidelberg Catechism, Q. 94), and the Apocrypha, 2 Maccabees included, are no part of Scripture (Westminster Confession 1.3). Their wording is about whom we may pray to, not about whom the saints pray for.
The Second London Baptist Confession (1689) limits prayer and worship to God alone (22.2) and says the books called Apocrypha are no part of the canon of Scripture (1.3).

title: Turn Away, Turn Back
sum: The chapter opens with the worst shame the ancient world could imagine: the bones of kings, priests and prophets dug out of their graves and spread under the sun and stars they worshiped. Then Jeremiah plays on one Hebrew word, shuv, "turn." A person who falls gets up; a person who turns away turns back. Judah turns away and keeps going. Birds know their seasons, but God's people do not know his order. The scribes' lying pen has turned the law into a lie, and prophet and priest cry "Peace, peace" when there is no peace.

From 8:13 the voice changes. The harvest fails, the people say "Why are we sitting still?", and an army sounds from Dan. Then Jeremiah speaks as a mourner: "Over the breaking of my dear people I am broken." The chapter ends on a question that has outlasted the book: "Is there no balm in Gilead? Is no healer there?"
readings: Read as one speech

Chapter 8 can be read as a single movement from judgment (8:1–17) to lament (8:18–22): the LORD speaks, the people speak, and the prophet breaks down. The unity makes the pun on turning and the question about healing the center of the chapter.
Read as a collection

Many scholars see separate poems joined by theme: a prose curse (8:1–3), a poem on turning (8:4–9), a repeated passage on false prophets (8:10–12, found also at 6:12–15), a harvest-and-army poem (8:13–17) and a lament (8:18–22). The Greek lacks 8:10b–12, which shows the repeated passage may be an addition.

views.H: The army "from Dan" (8:16) fits the years of the Babylonian threat after 605 BC. The exhumation of the leaders (8:1–2) came true in the sense that Jerusalem's kings and nobles were killed or exiled; the Bible does not report a literal digging up of Judah's graves, so some readers take it as a curse and not a forecast.
views.C: The repeat of 6:12–15 in 8:10b–12 is one of the best-known doublets in the book. The Greek lacks it here, and 4QJer-a has it, so the Greek's source either did not have it or omitted it. The word play on shuv is a mark of Jeremiah's poetry. Several words (8:13, 8:18) are uncertain in Hebrew and the Greek reads them differently.
views.J: The Jewish word for repentance, teshuvah, comes from the same root as shuv, "turn." The chapter's "Peace, peace" is the model of the false prophet's message. Jeremiah 8:13–9:23 in the Hebrew numbering (English 8:13–9:24) is the reading from the prophets on the morning of the Ninth of Av, when Jews mourn the Temple.
views.X: The question "Is there no balm in Gilead?" became the title of an African American spiritual that answers yes, and Christians have read the healer as Christ. The exchange with the false prophets "Peace, peace" is echoed in Paul's warning about "Peace and security" (1 Thessalonians 5:3).

deep.h: A repeated passage the Greek lacks
deep.b:
Verses 8:10b–12 repeat 6:12–15, and 4QJer-a, a Qumran copy that mostly follows the Masoretic edition, has them. The Greek lacks them. The usual explanation is that the longer Hebrew edition repeated a set piece and the Greek preserves the shorter text. In both places the verses call the leaders to account in the same words: they treat a wound as if it were nothing. Where the Hebrew is the same, the Plain English Translation gives the same English in both places (see 6:12–15). It keeps the real differences: in 8:10 the wives go "to other men" and the fields "to men who will take them over"; in 8:11 the people are the "daughter of my people"; in 8:12 the time is "the time of their punishment." The note at 8:11 lists them.

Other, smaller differences between the Hebrew and the Greek of this chapter (the missing "of Armies" in 8:3, the missing "declares the LORD" in 8:17) do not change the meaning and are not listed.

echoes: Jeremiah 6:13–15; Deuteronomy 30:19; 2 Kings 23:16; Psalm 58:4–5; Genesis 37:25; Ezekiel 27:17; 1 Thessalonians 5:3

settings.what: The curse of the open graves and the call to turn
settings.to: The people of Judah and Jerusalem, and their leaders
settings.when: In the years after the Temple sermon, under threat from the north
settings.why: To show that the nation's leaders and their gods will be shamed, and to ask why a people that knows how to rise from a fall refuses to turn back.
settings.readers: For the exiles, the chapter explained both the disaster and the false hope that preceded it.

settings.what: Against the scribes, the wise and the prophets who say all is well
settings.to: The scribes and teachers who say "We are wise, and the LORD's law is with us" (8:8), and the prophets and priests of 8:10b–12
settings.when: Not dated. 8:10b–12 repeats 6:12–15, so the words were used more than once
settings.why: To answer a claim of wisdom with a charge: those who handle the written law have made it into a lie, and prophets and priests treat a broken nation as if it had a scratch. Hearing it as aimed at the professionals, not at the whole nation, shows who is being named: the people who claimed authority over the law.

settings.what: The failed harvest and the army from Dan
settings.by: The LORD, with the people's own voice in 8:14–15
settings.to: The people of Judah and Jerusalem
settings.when: As the threat from the north draws near
settings.why: To make the people hear their own words, "Why are we sitting still?", and the sound of the horses from Dan, as the judgment they had been told would come.

settings.to: Heard by the people; spoken to the LORD and to himself
settings.when: As the Babylonian threat closes in, in the early years of Jehoiakim's reign or later
settings.why: To show the prophet suffering with the people he condemns, and so to make the judgment more believable. The grief is also an argument: the message is not the voice of a man who wants the nation to fall.

title: Weeping Prophet, Lying Tongues
sum: Jeremiah wishes his head were water and his eyes a fountain of tears, and then wishes he could leave his people altogether. Both wishes are true to the chapter. The people are a band of liars: every brother is a trickster, every neighbor a slanderer, and the tongue is a bow aimed at the next person. The LORD answers with a furnace ("I am about to smelt them") and a question: "Should I not take revenge on a nation like this?"

The second half calls for the professional mourners: "Send for the women who wail." Death has crept in through the windows. Then two verses lift the chapter from sorrow to a different sort of boasting: let no wise, strong or rich person boast, but let the one who boasts boast that he knows the LORD, who acts in loyal love, justice and righteousness. The chapter ends with a verdict that surprises: Egypt, Judah, Edom, Ammon, Moab and the desert tribes are all "uncircumcised," and Israel is uncircumcised in heart.
readings: Read as one man's grief
The poem is Jeremiah's own lament over a people he cannot save. It shows the prophet torn between loyalty to them and obedience to God, and it is the source of his reputation as the weeping prophet.
Read as the grief of God
Abraham Heschel and others hear God himself behind the tears. The same words ("my dear people") are the LORD's own in 9:7. The prophet weeps because he shares the feeling of the One who sent him.

views.H: The chapter belongs to the years of threat, when slander and betrayal were reported among the people (compare Jeremiah 20:10). The verses on circumcision (9:25–26) list neighbors, several of which Babylon later attacked, though the text does not name the conqueror.
views.C: The Hebrew verse numbers are one lower (English 9:1 is Hebrew 8:23). The Greek reads 9:6 differently ("interest on interest, deceit on deceit"), and the written and read forms differ in 9:8. The wording "circumcised in a foreskin" is a puzzle, and the verse on boasting is a model case of prophetic wisdom language.
views.J: Tradition makes Jeremiah the weeping prophet and the author of Lamentations (Bava Batra 15a). Rashi, on the verse the Hebrew numbers 9:25 (English 9:26), says the nations listed "were the neighbors of Eretz Israel, and they were punished shortly after her." Jewish readers have taken 9:23–24 as a summary of what God wants.
views.X: Paul turns 9:24 into "Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord" (1 Corinthians 1:31; 2 Corinthians 10:17). The circumcision of the heart in 9:26 is close to Paul's claim that the true Jew is one inwardly (Romans 2:28–29) and the church's picture of a spiritual circumcision (Colossians 2:11).

deep.h: The one passage about what to boast in
deep.b: Jeremiah 9:23–24 sets three goods the ancient world admired (wisdom, strength, riches) against one: to know the LORD. But the knowing is not private feeling. The LORD says he himself acts in loyal love, justice and righteousness, and "in these things I delight." To know him is to share his tastes. Jeremiah says the same of King Josiah, who judged the cause of the poor and needy, and the LORD asks whether that is not what knowing him means (22:15–16).

The final verses are a riddle, and the Hebrew gives no one answer. On the first reading, the verses assume that the neighbors were circumcised as Israel was. Jeremiah says that is not what matters. If the body is circumcised but the heart is not, the rite protects no one. Deuteronomy had already asked Israel to circumcise their hearts (Deuteronomy 10:16; 30:6). The question for the churches, whether baptism is the new circumcision, is discussed at Colossians 2:11 and under the topic on circumcision.

deep.h: Where the Greek differs in chapter 9
deep.b: The Greek has small differences that do not turn on a variant. In 9:14 the Hebrew "the Baals" is "idols" (eidola) in the Greek. In 9:6 the Greek has "interest on interest, and deceit on deceit" where the Hebrew has "deceit on deceit." In 9:26 the Greek list is Egypt, Idumaea, Edom, Ammon and Moab, and Judah is not named. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.

echoes: Jeremiah 8:21; Jeremiah 6:27–30; Genesis 25:26; Hosea 12:3; Jeremiah 22:15–16; 1 Corinthians 1:31; Romans 2:25–29; Deuteronomy 10:16

settings.by: Jeremiah and the LORD, speaking in turns
settings.to: The people of Judah, overheard, and God himself
settings.when: In the years of growing threat, before the first deportation of 597
settings.why: To show the cost of the people's lies and to explain in plain terms why the land will be laid waste: they have left the law and followed the Baals. The voices alternate so that the reader cannot tell where the prophet's grief ends and God's begins.

settings.what: The call to the wailing women
settings.to: The mourning women of Jerusalem, and through them the whole city
settings.when: On the eve of the disaster
settings.why: To tell the town to practice its funeral songs before they are needed. The call turns a common profession into a prophecy of mass death.

settings.what: A word on boasting and on circumcision
settings.to: Judah's elite who boast of wisdom, might and wealth, and the nation that trusts its circumcision
settings.when: Not dated; set among the oracles of the early years of Jehoiakim
settings.why: To say that no human advantage secures a nation, and that outward marks save no one. The audience is expected to hear that they are lumped with the neighbors they thought of as pagan.
settings.readers: For the exiles, the verses told how to boast when their wise men, army and wealth were gone.

title: No One Like You
sum: Chapter 10 is a sermon against idols that is half satire and half hymn. A tree is cut from the forest, shaped with a tool, decorated with silver and gold and nailed down so it will not wobble. It cannot speak or walk. It is a scarecrow in a cucumber patch. Do not be afraid of it, because it can do neither harm nor good. In contrast the LORD made the earth by his power, the world by his wisdom, and the sky by his understanding. When he gives his voice, waters roar in the heavens.

Then the chapter turns to the siege. Zion packs her bundle, her tent is torn, the shepherds have no sense, and a great noise comes from the north. The chapter ends with a prayer: "Correct me, LORD, but by what is just," and then "Pour out your fury on the nations that have not known you." Verse 11, in Aramaic, is the one line of the book that is not Hebrew.
readings: Read as a sermon for exiles

Many scholars think 10:1–16 was aimed at people living among Babylon's idols, perhaps the exiles, who needed words to reply to the pressure of foreign religion. The Aramaic sentence in 10:11 then becomes a ready reply in the language of the street.
Read as Jeremiah's own sermon in Judah

The chapter can also fit the years before 597, when Judah was already under the pressure of Babylon's gods and stars (10:2). Jeremiah's other words against idols (2:26–28; 16:19–20) agree, and the mocking style fits his style.

views.H: The warning about "signs in the sky" fits the Babylonian omen-watching that Judah met after 605 BC. If the foe from the north is Babylon, as is usually held, the northern din in 10:22 is its army. The prayer of 10:23–25 sounds like a request made as the siege came near.
views.C: Chapter 10 is the main test of the two editions. 4QJer-b and the Greek lack 10:6–8 and 10:10, 4QJer-a has 10:10, and Tov takes the shorter text as earlier. The mocking of idol-makers is similar to Isaiah 40–48, and how it relates to Jeremiah 10:1–16 is debated. Verses 10:12–16 are repeated in 51:15–19. Some scholars read the northern foe of 10:22 as the Scythians, as an older view held of the early chapters (see 4:6).
views.J: Rashi says 10:11 is a letter Jeremiah sent in Aramaic to Jeconiah and the exiles, to answer the Chaldeans if they were told to worship idols, and he cites Midrash Tanchuma (Shoftim 12) in connection with it.
views.X: Christians have read the chapter beside Paul's argument that an idol is nothing (1 Corinthians 8:4) and John's call to keep away from idols (1 John 5:21). The Letter of Jeremiah in the Catholic and Orthodox Bibles expands this chapter.

deep.b: Here the Dead Sea scrolls show both versions of Jeremiah in use at the same time. 4QJer-b, a copy from the second century BC (published estimates run from about 200 BC to the middle of the century), is preserved from 9:23 to 10:21. It has 10:1–5 and then 9 and 11 without 6–8 and 10, as the Greek does, and 4QJer-a has 10:10 as the Masoretic Text does. Both were found in Cave 4. Tov uses this as one of his main examples that the Greek translated an earlier, shorter Hebrew edition. A minority holds that the Greek translator cut the text. In the Plain English Translation, the long edition is the base and the omissions are shown as variants.

The satire gives the idols no credit. Ancient worshipers did not think the wood was the god. In their view a consecrated statue was where the god chose to be present, and rites of "opening the mouth" in Mesopotamia and Egypt made it so. Jeremiah's ridicule, like Isaiah's, is the case an outsider makes against a practice, not an account the worshipers would give. The point of the chapter does not depend on that fairness. It is to say that the nations' gods did not make the heavens and the earth (10:11).

echoes: Jeremiah 51:15–19; Psalm 135:7; Psalm 135:15–18; Isaiah 44:9–20; Isaiah 40:18–20; Baruch 6; Psalm 79:6–7; Habakkuk 2:18–19

settings.what: Sermon against idols and hymn to the Creator
settings.to: "The house of Israel" (10:1), whether the people of Judah or the exiles
settings.when: Undated. Some place it in the years under pressure from Babylon's religion, before 597; others, with the exiles in Babylon after 597
settings.why: To tell the people not to learn the nations' ways or fear their omens, and to set the living God against dead images. For people who saw Babylon's gods win, it said that victory does not make a god.
settings.readers: For later readers, the chapter gave a short creed that could be recited against idolatry.
views: The warnings against omens and the references to Judah's cities (10:17–22) suit the last years of the kingdom.
The Aramaic verse and the stress on foreign nations' gods fit people living in Babylon. Rashi calls 10:11 a letter to Jeconiah and the exiles.

settings.by: The LORD (10:17–18), then a speaker who may be Jeremiah, Zion or the nation (10:19–25)
settings.to: Zion under siege, and then the LORD
settings.when: As the northern army approaches, probably in the years before 597
settings.why: To tell the city to pack, to voice its grief, and to turn the cry into a prayer for correction and for justice on the nations that have eaten Jacob. It lets the audience hear their own suffering as a prayer.

title: The Covenant, the Plot, the Lamb
sum: The LORD tells Jeremiah to proclaim "the words of this covenant" in the cities of Judah and the streets of Jerusalem. The covenant goes back to the day the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt's iron furnace: listen to my voice and I will be your God. They did not listen. Now a plot has been found: Judah and Israel have gone back to the sins of their ancestors, and the LORD says he will bring a calamity they cannot escape and will not hear their cry. For the second time he tells Jeremiah not to pray for them (11:14; the first was 7:16).

From 11:18 the story becomes personal. Jeremiah did not know that people had planned to kill him. "I was like a tame lamb being led away to slaughter." The plotters are the men of his own village, Anathoth. He asks the LORD for justice. The LORD promises that the men of Anathoth will die, and none will be left.
readings: Read as the story of a prophet

The chapter moves from a public sermon to a private danger. The word that Jeremiah was told to cry in the streets gets him marked for death at home. The covenant he proclaimed is the reason he is hated.
Read as a covenant lawsuit

The chapter has the pattern of a covenant case: the terms (11:3–4), the history of obedience refused (11:7–8), the charge of treason (11:9–10), the sentence (11:11–17). The plot against Jeremiah then becomes a second case, in which the prophet is the plaintiff.

views.H: The most likely setting is after Josiah's covenant of 622 BC (2 Kings 23:1–3), when the book of the covenant was read in the cities. Whether Jeremiah supported the reform or only used its language is debated. The sins of the "ancestors" repeated in 11:10 are the idol worship of Manasseh's reign (2 Kings 21).
views.C: Verses 11:1–14 are prose in the style of Deuteronomy, and many scholars attribute them to the Deuteronomistic editors, working on a core of Jeremiah's words. The Greek lacks 11:7 and most of 11:8. 11:15 is one of the hardest verses in the book. 11:18–12:6 is usually counted as the first of Jeremiah's "confessions."
views.J: Rashi explains the plot to "destroy the tree with its bread" as a plan to poison his food. Rashi also reports that Targum Jonathan reads the lamb as a "choice lamb."
views.X: Early Christian writers read 11:19 as speaking of Christ: the lamb led to slaughter and the wood put in his bread. Justin (Dialogue with Trypho 72) already quotes the line as Jeremiah's, and Tertullian (Against Marcion 3.19) reads the wood as the cross. The reading depends on the Greek wording and goes beyond what Jeremiah himself says. Jeremiah's suffering is also read as a foretaste of the Passion without a claim that the verse predicts it.

deep.h: Why did Anathoth want him dead?
deep.b: Chapter 11 gives the plotters' words but not their motive. The text gives no motive; commentators suggest four. (1) They resented his Temple sermon and its threat to the Temple, the source of a priest's living. (2) Jeremiah had supported Josiah's reform, which closed local sanctuaries and left priests like those at Anathoth without income (2 Kings 23:8–9). (3) They were of Abiathar's line, whom Solomon had banished (1 Kings 2:26–27), and may have resented the Jerusalem priesthood and a prophet who spoke for its Temple. (4) They simply could not bear what he said: do not prophesy in the LORD's name. Only the last is stated by the text.

deep.h: Tame lamb, or lamb and ox
deep.b: The word aluf is the clue. It can mean "tame," as in a pet lamb, or "ox, leader," and Rashi reports that Dunash and Judah ben Kudish took it as "a lamb and an ox," while Menahem took "aluf" as "large." The Greek has "innocent lamb" (arnion akakon). Whatever the exact word, the picture is of an animal that trusts its keeper and does not know where it is being led. Jeremiah's point is his innocence.

In 11:6 the Greek has "outside Jerusalem" where the Hebrew has "in the streets of Jerusalem." The meaning of the command, to cry the words of the covenant to the whole land, does not change, so it is not listed as a variant. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.

echoes: Jeremiah 7:16; Jeremiah 14:11; Jeremiah 20:12; 2 Kings 23:1–3; Deuteronomy 27:15–26; Isaiah 53:7; Acts 8:32; Romans 11:17–24

settings.to: The people of Judah and Jerusalem, and in verse 14 Jeremiah alone. Verses 15–17 turn to poetry addressed to a feminine singular "beloved" (Judah, as the LORD's beloved)
settings.when: Not dated. Many place it after Josiah's covenant of 622 BC, when the covenant words were being read; some think the prose is later
settings.why: To remind a people who believed the covenant protected them that it also carried curses, and to say they had already broken it by returning to the sins of their ancestors. The audience is told they are guilty of treason against their king, the LORD.
settings.readers: For the exiles, it explained the fall as covenant curse, not divine defeat.
views: Jeremiah preaches the words of the law book to a nation that has just sworn to keep them.
The prose reflects Deuteronomistic editing after the fall of Jerusalem, built on an older core.

settings.what: The plot against Jeremiah (first of the confessions)
settings.by: Jeremiah, in prayer, and the LORD's answer
settings.to: The LORD; the answer concerns the men of Anathoth
settings.when: After his sermons began to anger his neighbors, perhaps in Jehoiakim's early years
settings.why: To show what the prophet's message cost him and to record that God took his side. For readers, the prayer shows that a prophet could argue with God and be answered.

title: Why Do the Wicked Prosper?
sum: Jeremiah brings the LORD a case. "You are righteous, LORD, whenever I bring a case to you. Even so, I want to speak with you about what is just: Why does the way of the wicked go well?" It is the question of Job and Psalm 73. The LORD gives no explanation. He says: if you are tired out by men running on foot, how will you race horses? If you feel safe only in a land of peace, what will you do in the Jordan's thick brush? And then he adds that Jeremiah's own brothers and father's house have betrayed him.

Then the LORD begins to speak of his own grief: "I have left my house. I have given up my inheritance." His people have become a lion that roars at him. The shepherds have wrecked the vineyard. The chapter ends with a promise that surprises: the wicked neighbors who touched Israel's land will be uprooted, and then the LORD will have compassion on them too. If they learn to swear by his name, they will be built up among his people.
readings: Read as the prophet's personal crisis

The chapter is the first of the confessions, where the prophet argues with God about justice without giving him up. God's reply, that things will get harder, tells him not to expect comfort. It shapes the later confessions.
Read as a divine lament

From 12:7 the LORD speaks in the first person, and the chapter becomes less about Jeremiah's pain than God's: his house abandoned, his vineyard wrecked, his heritage a roaring lion. The prophet's pain is a window on God's.

views.H: The drought and invasions of 12:4, 12:7–13 may reflect raids on Judah around 601–598 BC, when Babylon sent bands of Chaldeans, Arameans, Moabites and Ammonites against Jehoiakim (2 Kings 24:2). The "wicked neighbors" of 12:14 are such neighbors.
views.C: 12:1–6 is the second part of the first confession (11:18–12:6). 12:7–13 is a divine lament and is often treated as a separate poem. 12:14–17 is prose, perhaps late, and adds the surprising offer to the nations. The Greek differs at 12:4 ("God will not see our ways") and 12:9 ("hyena's cave").
views.J: Rashi hears 12:4's "he will not see our end" as the wicked saying God does not know what will happen to them. The chapter is read as the model of how a righteous person may question God. Mishnah Avot (numbered 4:15 in many editions) has Rabbi Yannai say that it is not in our power to explain the prosperity of the wicked or the suffering of the righteous.
views.X: Christians read Jeremiah's betrayal by kin beside Jesus' rejection by his own family and town (Mark 3:21; 6:4; John 7:5). Verse 12:2, "near in their mouth, far from their kidneys," is close to the words of Isaiah on lip service that Jesus quotes (Matthew 15:8).

deep.b: God's reply (12:5) is not an answer. A reader may find it hard, even rude. Some commentators hear in it a sign that the prophet's call will cost more than he thought. Others note that God does not scold him for asking: the complaint itself becomes part of the conversation with God, and Jeremiah's lament is kept in the book as an example. The question is taken up again in 15:10–21, 17:14–18, 18:18–23 and 20:7–18, with a different answer each time.

The last verses use the verb of Jeremiah's call, "uproot" (1:10), on the nations that attacked Judah, and then give them the same hope as Judah. They may learn the ways of the LORD's people and be "built up." If not, the uprooting is final. Isaiah 19:24–25 goes further and names Egypt and Assyria as the LORD's people.

echoes: Jeremiah 11:18–23; Jeremiah 20:12; Job 21; Psalm 73; Habakkuk 1:2–4; Isaiah 29:13; Matthew 15:8; Isaiah 19:24–25; Jeremiah 1:10; Jeremiah 18:7–10

settings.what: Jeremiah's complaint and the LORD's reply
settings.to: The LORD; overheard by the readers
settings.why: To ask why the wicked do well and to be told that harder days are coming. It tells later readers that doubt is part of prophetic faith, and that the LORD does not remove it with a theory.

settings.what: The LORD's lament over his house and land
settings.to: Heard by Jeremiah and the people of Judah
settings.when: In the years of raids and drought around the reign of Jehoiakim
settings.why: To say that God also suffers, and that his people's judgment is not his satisfaction but his loss. For the people, it is a reason to listen.

settings.what: Judgment on the neighbors, and an offer
settings.to: Judah, and the nations that touched its land
settings.when: Undated; possibly after the raids on Judah in Jehoiakim's time, or added later
settings.why: To tell Judah that its enemies will answer to God too, and to tell the nations that they can be part of his people. For exiles it widened the hope.
views: The verses match his commission over nations (1:10).
The prose style and the offer to the nations have been taken as a late editor's addition.
